extracted.subtask_short: PTAB IPR/PGR guidance for patent owners
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and procedural standards for Patent Owners responding to inter partes reviews (IPRs) and post-grant reviews (PGRs) before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) in the United States. Covers eligibility, timing, petition requirements, burdens/standards, discovery, motions to amend, hearings, estoppel, settlement, and appeal/rehearing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB composition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Trial and Appeal Board ("PTAB" or "Board") is a tribunal of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office ("PTO") that assesses the institution and trial of IPRs and PGRs. The PTAB includes statutory members (PTO Director, Deputy Director, Commissioner for Patents) and administrative patent judges ("APJs"). Panels of three APJs typically decide each IPR and PGR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APJs are Article I judges with technical backgrounds and PTO registration; panels are technically savvy and prepare extensively for hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of IPRs and PGRs
rubrics_metrics.description: An inter partes review ("IPR") or post-grant review ("PGR") is a proceeding that permits a Petitioner to attack the validity of one or more claims of an issued patent. These proceedings only examine validity and do not adjudicate infringement, award damages, injunctions, or other remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They were created by the American Invents Act (AIA); provisions governing IPRs and PGRs took effect on September 16, 2012.

rubrics_metrics.name: Window of vulnerability / eligibility for PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: PGRs: only patents with at least one AIA claim (priority date on or after March 16, 2013) are eligible, and a Petitioner must bring a PGR within nine months of issuance (or re-issuance) of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent lacks an AIA claim it is ineligible for PGR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Window of vulnerability / eligibility for IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: IPRs: all patents are eligible and there is no general deadline for filing an IPR. However, if the patent has at least one AIA claim, the Petitioner must wait to file until the later of nine months after issuance (or re-issuance) or termination of any PGR on the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Petitioner has been served with a complaint for patent infringement, a strict one-year deadline to file a petition applies (35 U.S.C. §315(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of attacks permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR: the only attacks a Petitioner can make are anticipation (35 U.S.C. §102) and obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103) based upon patents and printed publications. PGR: in addition to anticipation and obviousness, a Petitioner can attack based on lack of written description (35 U.S.C. §112), indefiniteness (35 U.S.C. §112), lack of enablement (35 U.S.C. §112), and eligibility (35 U.S.C. §101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under certain circumstances the PTAB may address eligibility of proposed amended claims under 35 U.S.C. §101 (see Uniloc2017LLC v. Hulu LLC precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file a petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who is not the owner of the patent may file an IPR or PGR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. Government is not a "person" for this purpose and thus cannot bring an IPR or PGR (ReturnMail, Inc. v. United States Postal Service).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay with district court litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Petitioner (and any real party in interest) cannot have previously filed a civil action in district court challenging the validity of the same patent; a Petitioner must choose whether to initially attack validity in district court or before the PTAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Petitioner can file a civil action for a declaratory judgment of noninfringement without hindering ability to concurrently or subsequently challenge validity before the PTAB. Filing a counterclaim for declaratory judgment of invalidity does not bar a subsequent IPR or PGR. Consider stays, estoppel, and timing when district court litigation is ongoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution thresholds and burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: For an IPR to be instituted, the Petition must demonstrate a reasonable likelihood that the Petitioner will prevail as to at least one challenged claim (may encompass a 50/50 chance). For a PGR to be instituted, the Petition must demonstrate that it is more likely than not that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable (greater than 50% chance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden of proof in IPRs and PGRs is 'preponderance of the evidence' (lighter burden) whereas in district court and ITC it is 'clear and convincing' (heavier burden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Director/Board discretion on institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the Petition meets statutory thresholds, the Board (or Director) has discretion whether to institute a trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include efficiency of the process, fundamental fairness, and whether the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments were previously presented to the Office (see 35 U.S.C. §§315(d), 325(d)). The PTAB will either institute on all claims and grounds alleged or deny institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition formal and substantive requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A Petition is a written document that may only attack one patent and must set forth the grounds for standing, the claim(s) attacked, the statutory grounds for the attack, how the claims are to be construed, and how/why the construed claim is unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions must identify real parties-in-interest, related matters, lead and back-up counsel, and service information, and are typically supported by one or more expert declarations and exhibits. Petitions have word limits: 14,000 words for IPRs and 18,700 words for PGRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims in IPRs and PGRs are construed using the same claim construction standard as in a civil action in district court: 'ordinary and customary meaning of such claims as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.' (37 C.F.R. §42.100(b); Phillips v. AWH Corp.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of the district-court standard affects how claim scope and prior art are assessed in the PTAB proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical review and filing date notice
rubrics_metrics.description: After filing, PTAB staff review the Petition for procedural compliance; if the Petition meets clerical criteria the PTAB issues a Notice of Being Accorded a Filing Date which starts the timeline. If not, the PTAB issues a Notice of deficiencies and a deadline for correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely correction of clerical deficiencies is critical to start the statutory timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-level timeline for proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Two major phases: a pre-institution phase (up to six months) and a post-institution or 'trial' phase (up to twelve months, absent special circumstances), with the entire proceeding generally taking eighteen months or less from filing date to Final Written Decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key milestone clocks include: 21 days for Mandatory Notices, up to 3 months for optional Preliminary Response, up to 3 months for institution decision after Preliminary Response deadline, 3 months for Patent Owner Response after institution, 3 months for Petitioner Reply, ~1 month for Patent Owner Sur-Reply, motions and hearings, and typically Final Written Decision within 3 months of Oral Hearing. Certain deadlines can be extended for good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory notices and first deadline (21 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 21 days of service of the Petition the Patent Owner must file Mandatory Notices: the real party-in-interest, related matters, lead and back-up counsel, and service information (37 C.F.R. §42.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Power of Attorney must also be filed unless designated counsel is already of record (37 C.F.R. §42.10(b)). Choose PTAB counsel quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel registration and use of district court attorneys
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead counsel in IPRs and PGRs must be registered to practice at the PTO; a district court attorney who is not a registered patent attorney may serve as back-up counsel if admitted pro hac vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB generally permits pro hac vice admission upon showing good cause (experience, familiarity). Consider Protective Order in district court proceedings when deciding counsel roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing Petition defects (procedural attacks)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the outset, consider whether the Petition contains fundamental flaws, such as the Petitioner having missed its one-year deadline after being served with a complaint (35 U.S.C. §315(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying procedural defects early can be a basis for dismissal or denial of institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for technical expert(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owner Responses (and some Preliminary Responses) are typically supported by at least one detailed declaration of a technical expert because PTAB APJs have technical backgrounds and the assessment of patentability is rigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain experts early. Experts should have extensive experience in the subject matter, be able to provide detailed declarations stating opinions and bases, and be prepared for deposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to amend: availability and burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owners have the option to propose substitute claims (generally on a claim-for-claim basis), but Motions to Amend are rarely granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules (amended Jan 2021): Patent Owner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the motion to amend complies' with statutory/regulatory requirements; Petitioner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable.' The Board may exercise discretion to grant or deny a motion to amend only for reasons 'supported by readily identifiable and persuasive evidence of record.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral Hearing preparation and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The Oral Hearing is one of very few opportunities to interact with the APJ panel; preparation is a must and requires in-depth familiarity with the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APJs know the record inside and out; litigants must be prepared to respond to interrogation. Demonstrative exhibits are often submitted prior to the hearing but may not include new evidence. PTAB may conduct hearings via video.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Written Decision content and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Within three months of the Oral Hearing the panel will issue its Final Written Decision which addresses all bases and claims raised in the Petition and patentability of any proposed amended claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final Written Decisions typically address claim construction, weight given to experts' opinions, fact-findings regarding scope and content of prior art, the Panel's judgment on disputed evidence, and reasoning behind conclusions as to patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A party dissatisfied with the Final Written Decision may file a single request for rehearing within 30 days of the entry of a final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The motion must specifically identify matters the movant believes the Board misapprehended or overlooked and indicate where in the record each matter was previously addressed. Requests for rehearing on institution decisions have shorter deadlines (14 or 30 days depending on context) and are rarely granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to Federal Circuit and standard of review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit reviews Board decisions under the Administrative Procedures Act, which requires setting aside Board conclusions that are 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law,' or 'unsupported by substantial evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals challenge factual findings or legal conclusions under APA standards (see Alacritech, Inc. v. Intel Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement and PTAB's ability to continue
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties can settle, but the PTAB has the right to step into the shoes of the Petitioner and proceed with the patentability analysis. The earlier in the process the proceeding is, the less likely the PTAB is to continue without both parties; conversely, further along increases the likelihood the PTAB will finish its analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timing of settlement and PTAB discretion when negotiating resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel effects on district court proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: If an IPR or PGR results in a Final Written Decision, a Petitioner (or real party in interest or privy of the Petitioner) may not assert in district court or in the ITC that any claim 'is invalid on any ground that the petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised' during the IPR or PGR (35 U.S.C. §§315(e)(2), 325(e)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PTAB now institutes on 'all challenged claims, all grounds' basis, instituted trials can have broad estoppel effects. If trial is not instituted, those grounds may be raised in district court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel effects on other PTO proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The outcome of an IPR or PGR may impact other PTO proceedings; Patent Owners are precluded from taking action in the PTO inconsistent with an adverse judgment, including obtaining a claim that is not patentably distinct from a finally-refused or cancelled claim (37 C.F.R. §42.73(d)(3)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate post-PTAB prosecution strategy with outcomes and potential estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery: scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery is permitted but limited compared to district court. 'Routine discovery' includes: (1) production of any exhibit cited in a paper or testimony; (2) cross-examination of the other side's declarants; and (3) relevant information that is inconsistent with a position advanced during the proceeding (PTAB Consolidated Trial Practice Guide).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain additional discovery, PTAB allows narrowly-tailored requests: for IPRs, further discovery where it 'furthers the interests of justice' (35 U.S.C. §316(a)(5); 37 C.F.R. §42.51(b)(2)); for PGRs, where 'good cause' is shown and limited to evidence directly related to factual assertions (35 U.S.C. §326(a)(5); 37 C.F.R. §42.224).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB has a default Protective Order. If either party wants a different Protective Order, there are procedures to obtain a different Order and the PTAB generally allows different Orders if the need is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider interplay between district court protective orders and PTAB protective order requests when confidential materials are at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition word limits and single-patent requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions have word limits (14,000 words for IPRs and 18,700 words for PGRs) and may only attack one patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to word limits and single-patent restriction; supporting declarations and exhibits are typical and must be tailored to the claimed grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution practice and statistical likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB historically institutes trials frequently and many claims have been 'killed' by the PTAB; institution rates and claim outcome statistics vary by technology and year (USPTO Trial Statistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Owners should take petitions seriously, choose PTAB counsel quickly, and consider early defensive strategies (e.g., preliminary response, early expert retention).
